title: Crawford v. Weather Shield Mfg., Inc. (2008) 44 Cal.4th 541 (contractual duty to defend under an indemnity agreement)
publisher: Opinion of the Supreme Court of California; text read on CourtListener, a Free Law Project reproduction
claims: The opinion, by Justice Baxter with six justices concurring, affirms the judgment of the Court of Appeal and disapproves Regan Roofing Co. v. Superior Court (1994) 24 Cal.App.4th 425 to the extent it conflicts with the opinion.

The opinion opens by stating that standard comprehensive liability insurance policies provide that the insurer must both indemnify and defend the insured against claims within the scope of the policy coverage, that the insurer's duty to defend is broader than its duty to indemnify, and that the duty to defend extends to claims that are merely potentially covered.
The court states that it addresses the contractual duty to defend in a noninsurance context, in a pre-2006 residential construction subcontract between a window supplier and a developer-builder.

The court concludes that the subcontract obliged the subcontractor to defend the developer in suits alleging construction defects arising from the subcontractor's negligence, even though a jury ultimately found the subcontractor was not negligent and the parties accepted an interpretation of the subcontract that gave the builder no right of indemnity unless the subcontractor was negligent.

The court states that parties to a construction contract have great freedom, subject to public policy and established rules of contract interpretation, to allocate indemnity and defense responsibilities, and may agree that the promisor's indemnity or defense obligations will apply only if the promisor was negligent, or even if the promisor was not negligent.
The opinion quotes Civil Code section 2772: 'Indemnity is a contract by which one engages to save another from a legal consequence of the conduct of one of the parties, or of some other person.'

The court states that although indemnity agreements resemble liability insurance policies, the rules for interpreting the two classes of contracts differ significantly: ambiguities in an insurance policy are construed against the insurer, while in noninsurance contexts the indemnitee may often have the superior bargaining power.

The court states that it has been said that if one seeks, in a noninsurance agreement, to be indemnified for his or her own active negligence, or regardless of the indemnitor's fault, the language must be particularly clear and explicit and will be construed strictly against the indemnitee.

The court states that at the time the subcontract was made a party to a construction contract could not validly agree to indemnify the promisee for the latter's sole negligence or willful misconduct, citing Civil Code section 2782(a) and section 1668.

The court states that section 2778 sets forth general rules for the interpretation of indemnity contracts unless a contrary intention appears, and that, if not forbidden by other more specific statutes, those obligations are deemed included in every indemnity agreement unless the parties indicate otherwise.

The court states that subdivision 4 of section 2778 places in every indemnity contract, unless the agreement provides otherwise, a duty to assume the indemnitee's defense, if tendered, against all claims embraced by the indemnity, and that this duty is distinct and separate from the obligation under subdivision 3 to pay an indemnitee's defense costs after the fact as part of any indemnity owed.

The court states that the duty to defend under subdivision 4 of section 2778 arises immediately upon a proper tender of defense by the indemnitee, before the litigation has determined whether indemnity is actually owed, and extends to claims which, at the time of tender, allege facts that would give rise to a duty of indemnity.

In a footnote the court states that it does not suggest the indemnitor's duty to defend would continue if all claims potentially subject to the indemnity were eliminated during the third party proceeding, or if the promisor conclusively established that the claims were not embraced by the indemnity, and that it expresses no view on those issues.

The court states that parties to an indemnity contract can easily disclaim any responsibility of the indemnitor for the indemnitee's defense or its costs, or can specify that the indemnitor's sole defense obligation will be to reimburse defense costs.

The opinion recites policy arguments by the subcontractor and its amici, including that small subcontractors lack the resources to fund a developer's defense up front while defending themselves in the same lawsuit, states that the court is sensitive to those policy issues, and declines the holding they propose.

The court notes that statutes effective January 1, 2006 and January 1, 2008 apply to residential construction contracts entered after their effective dates and void terms obliging a subcontractor to indemnify certain other project participants, including the cost to defend, against construction defect claims to the extent the claims arise out of, pertain to, or relate to the negligence of those other entities; the opinion cites them by the subdivision letters of section 2782 in force at the time.
updateCadence: Static once filed; its effect can be changed by later decisions or legislation, and the statutory subdivisions it cites have since been renumbered.
